description_en: The Kākrēvihāra Temple sits on top of a densely forested hill located 3 km south of Birendranagar, the Surkhet district headquarters, and 2 km southeast of the 16th century Lāṭīkoilī Temple (SRK0030).The monument was in a state of ruin, with blocks scattered over a large area, until the 2000's. The Department of Archaeology has undertaken the full reconstruction of the temple since then.The temple is (re)built on a cruciform platform and itself has a cruciform plan oriented to the four cardinal directions. Steps are placed at the centre of each sides of the platform. Large doors are placed on each side of the building. They lead to a singlesanctum. The elevation of the temple that was reconstituted by the Department of Archaeology rendered aśekhari śikharastructure, which consists of a centralśikharatower against which miniature towers (kūṭa) are leaning. It is the onlyśekhari śikharastructure known for the Karnali region.The facades are covered with rich stone sculptures representing Buddhist themes such as the Jātakas, the Buddha's life scenes, etc. Dilli Raj Sharma identified representations of the Śrāvasti Miracle, a Tārā, scenes of the Khumba and Nigraodhamiga Jātakas (Sharma 2012, 129-166).Jason Hawkes et al. have proposed to date the temple from Ripumalla's period, i.e. in the 1310's (Hawkes et al. 2012). This dating does however not agree with the architectural and artistic features of the monument. Indeed, its elevation as well as its art are almost identical to that of the Gujjar Deva Temple in Dwarahat, Uttarakhand, which Nachiket Chanchani dated from 1075-1150 (Chanchani 2019). Together, the Gujjar Deva and Kākrēvihāra temples attest to the presence, between the 10th and 12th centuries, of artists and architects from western India who were carrying the so-called Māru-Gurjara style in the Himalayan hills of the Mahakali and Karnali basins (Andolfatto 2019;2022).
